mjólk_no.etymology:
From Old Norse mjǫlk, mjolk, from Proto-Germanic *meluks, cognate with Danish mælk, Swedish mjölk, English milk. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ-.
Note the lack of i-mutation in the genitive (from *melukiz). Although the form would suggest a mutated **mýlkur, -jó- is not the original vowel (from *-eu-, as in þjóð), but a product of a double vowel change, first fracture: meluk- > mjǫlk, and then lengthening: o/ǫ > ó before lk. Also, the ability of the -iz to effect an i-mutation on the first vowel is reduced by the intermediate -u-.

svangur_lo.etymology:
From Old Norse svangr (“slender, slim, thin”), from Proto-Germanic *swangaz (“thin, slim”). The original meaning in Germanic was probably 'curved inwards', discernible from the derived Old Norse svangi (“flank, groin”), i.e., 'the sides of the abdomen which curve inwards slightly'. Within Icelandic the meaning developed from 'thin' to 'feeling hungry'. Cognates are Faroese svangur (“hungry”), Danish svang (“thin, famished”), Norwegian svang (“hungry”), dialectal Swedish svånger (“thin, hungry, empty”), Middle Swedish svanger (“slender, emaciated, very thin”), Middle High German swanger (“flexible, slender”).
Further origin unsure, perhaps related to Middle Irish seng (“narrow, thin”). Not related to Danish svanger, Norwegian svanger, Dutch zwanger, German schwanger (“pregnant”).

nokkur_fn.etymology: From Old Norse nǫkkurr, from earlier nakkvarr, from Proto-Norse *ᚾᛁ ᚹᚨᛁᛏ ᛖᚲ ᚺᚹᚨᚱᛃᚨᛉ (*ni wait ek hwarjaʀ, literally “not-know-I-who”).

hálfur_lo.etymology: From Old Norse halfr, from Proto-Germanic *halbaz.

hús_no.etymology: From Old Norse hús, from Proto-Germanic *hūsą.

heimili_no.etymology: From Old Norse heimili (“home”), a formation related to heimr (“realm, region”).

borg_no.etymology: From Old Norse borg, from Proto-Germanic *burgz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ-. Related to berg, bjarg (“rock, cliff”).

en: land, earth, ground (part of the Earth not under water)
land, as a mass noun, measurable in quantity
land_no.etymology: From Old Norse land, from Proto-Germanic *landą, from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”).

gata_no.etymology: From Old Norse gata, from Proto-Germanic *gatwǭ.

vegur_no.etymology: From Old Norse vegr, Proto-Germanic *wegaz, from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-. Cognate with Latin via.

búð_no.etymology: From Old Norse búð, a variant of *bóð, from Proto-Germanic *bōþō (“building, dwelling”).

skóli_no.etymology: Borrowed from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ).

bíll_no.etymology: Borrowed from Danish bil, a shortened form of automobil, ultimately from Ancient Greek αὐτός (autós, “self”), stem αὐτo- (auto-) + Latin mōbilis (“mobile”), ergo ‘[vehicle] which moves by itself’.

hjól_no.etymology: From Old Norse hjól, originally the plural of hvel.

bátur_no.etymology: From Old Norse bátr, from Old English bāt (“boat”). Doublet of beit, directly inherited from Proto Germanic.

kirkja_no.etymology: From Old Norse kirkja, from Old English cirice.

safn_no.etymology: From safna, from Old Norse safna, a by-form of samna (“to collect, assemble”), from Proto-Germanic *samnōną (“to gather, collect”). More at sam.

garður_no.etymology: From Old Norse garðr, from Proto-Germanic *gardaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰórdʰos < *gʰerdʰ-.

kort_no.etymology: Inherited from Old Norse kort (“a map”), from Middle High German karte, from Old French carte, from Latin charta (“papyrus, paper”). Related to Danish kort (“a map”) and German Karte (“a card; a map”).

hægri_lo.etymology: From Old Norse hǿgri, comparative of hǿgr (“easy, convenient”), from Proto-Germanic *hōgiz. Cognates with the Danish højre and Swedish högra, höger.

vinstri_lo.etymology: From Old Norse vinstri, from Proto-Germanic *winistraz. Cognates with Old High German winstar, Danish venstre and Swedish vänster.

hér_ao.etymology: From Old Norse hér (“here”), from Proto-Germanic *hē₂r.

þar_ao.etymology: From Old Norse þar, from Proto-Germanic *þar.

hvar_ao.etymology: From Old Norse hvar, from Proto-Germanic *hwar.

norður_ao.etymology: From Old Norse norðr, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrą.

suður_ao.etymology: From Old Norse suðr, from Proto-Germanic *sunþrą.

en: east, eastward (designating movement to the east)
in the east (only used together with a prepositional phrase indicating a more precise location, except when used comparatively)
austur_ao.etymology: From Old Norse austr, from Proto-Germanic *austrą.

vestur_ao.etymology: From Old Norse vestr, from Proto-Germanic *westrą.

en: to fit, to go, to be satisfactory, to do
ganga_so.etymology: From Old Norse ganga, from Proto-Germanic *ganganą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰengʰ-.

keyra_so.etymology: From Old Norse keyra, from Proto-Germanic *kaurijaną, whence also Danish køre (“to drive, travel”). No known direct correspondence in West or East Germanic, but perhaps cognate with English chare, German kehren, or with Serbo-Croatian журити (се)/žúriti (se) (“to hurry”).

finna_so.etymology: From Old Norse finna, from Proto-Germanic *finþaną, from Proto-Indo-European *pent- (“to go, pass; path, bridge”).

en: to seek, to search, to look for

beygja_so.etymology: From Old Norse beygja, from Proto-Germanic *baugijaną.

en: to wait, pile up, be on the docket
to await, wait for; to be on someone's to-do list
bíða_so.etymology: From Old Norse bíða, from Proto-Germanic *bīdaną. The irregular supine beðið is probably the result of contamination with the verb biðja (“to bid”).

í_fs.etymology: From Old Norse í, from Proto-Germanic *in, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én.

á_fs.etymology: From Old Norse á, from Proto-Norse ᚨᚾ (an), from Proto-Germanic *ana.

til_fs.etymology: From Old Norse til, from Proto-Germanic *til (compare *tilą (“goal”)).

en: adverbial form of preposition, used in compounds
frá_fs.etymology: From Old Norse frá, from Proto-Germanic *fram.

en: by, near, next to, at (someone's) place

úr_fs.etymology: From Old Norse ór (“out of”), from Proto-Germanic *uz (“out, out of”). More at Old English or-.

yfir_fs.etymology: From Old Norse yfir, from Proto-Germanic *ubiri, from Proto-Indo-European *upéri, from *upér, from *upo. Related to of (“too”) and ofan (“from above”).

undir_fs.etymology: From Old Norse undir, from Proto-Germanic *under.

tími_no.etymology: From Old Norse tími, from Proto-Germanic *tīmô (“time”), from Proto-Indo-European *tī-, from *dī- (“time”).

vika_no.etymology: From Old Norse vika, from Proto-Germanic *wikǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *weyg- (“to bend, wind, turn, yield”).

mánuður_no.etymology: From Old Norse mánuðr, variant of mánaðr, from Proto-Germanic *mēnōþs (“month”), from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon, month”). See also máni. Cognate with Faroese mánaður, Danish and Norwegian Bokmål måned and Swedish and Norwegian Nynorsk månad, English month, Old English mōnaþ, German Monat, Dutch maand.

ár_no.etymology: Inherited from Old Norse ár (“year”), from Proto-Germanic *jērą, from Proto-Indo-European *yeh₁r-. Cognates include: Dutch jaar and Afrikaans jaar, English year, German Jahr, Danish år, Norwegian Bokmål år and Swedish år.

klukka_no.etymology: From Old Norse klokka, from Latin clocca.

en: weekend; more generally, two or more holidays in a row, in conjunction with a Sunday or a major Christian holiday
helgi_no.etymology: From Old Norse helgr (accusative and dative helgi).

mánudagur_no.etymology: From Old Norse mánadagr, from Proto-West Germanic *mānini dag, a calque of Latin dies lunae. Compare Faroese mánadagur, Danish and Norwegian Bokmål mandag, Swedish and Norwegian Nynorsk måndag.

miðvikudagur_no.etymology: From mið (“middle”) + vika (“week”) + dagur (“day”). Compare German Mittwoch (“Wednesday”).

sunnudagur_no.etymology: From sunna (“sun”) + dagur (“day”). From Old Norse sunnudagr, from Proto-West Germanic *sunnōn dag, a calque of Latin dies Solis.

sumar_no.etymology: From Old Norse sumar (neuter), earlier sumarr (masculine), from Proto-Germanic *sumaraz.

vetur_no.etymology: From Old Norse vetr (“winter, year”), from Proto-Germanic *wintruz.

haust_no.etymology: From Old Norse haust from earlier haustr (masculine), from Proto-Germanic *harbustaz, *harbistaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kerp-. Compare Old English hærfest, English harvest, the Old High German Herbist; German Herbst, Danish høst and Swedish höst.

núna_ao.etymology: From Old Norse nú (“now”), from Proto-Germanic *nu.

oft_ao.etymology: From Old Norse oft (“often”), opt (“oft, often”), from Proto-Germanic *ufta, *uftō (“often”).

snemma_ao.etymology: From Old Norse snemma, snimma, from Proto-Germanic *sneumô. Cognate with Faroese snimma.

byrja_so.etymology: From Old Norse byrja, from Proto-Germanic *burjaną.

en: to quit, stop, cease, cut out, discontinue
hætta_so.etymology: From Old Norse hætta, from Proto-Germanic *hanhtijaną. In the sense “stop” an unstressed prefix has likely been dropped, perhaps *ab-.

sofa_so.etymology: From Old Norse sofa, from Proto-Germanic *swefaną. Unrelated to English sofa.

vakna_so.etymology: From Old Norse vakna, from Proto-Germanic *waknaną. By surface analysis, vakinn (“awake”) + -a (inchoative suffix)

um_fs.etymology: Inherited from Old Norse um, inherited from Proto-Germanic *umbi (“around, about”).

en: after, in (temporal; e.g., after three days)
eftir_fs.etymology: From Old Norse eptir, eptr, from Proto-Germanic *aftiri (“more aft, further behind”), *after, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epóteros (“further behind, further away”), comparative form of *h₂epó (“off, behind”).

en: for, before (describing a target deadline or time frame)
for (expressing an amount paid for an object)
to/for (expressing perception or benefit with some adjectives)
fyrir_fs.etymology: From Old Norse fyrir (“before, for”), from Proto-Germanic *furi (“before, for”).

þegar_st.etymology: From Old Norse þegar, cognate with Old Swedish þaghar, Old Gutnish þegar.

en: march (musical piece such as is played while marching)
mars_no.etymology: Borrowed from Latin mārtiī, genitive singular of mārtius (“relating to Mars”), from Mārs (“Mars, Roman god of war and agriculture”).

en: September (the ninth month of the Gregorian calendar, following August and preceding October, containing the southward equinox)
November (the eleventh month of the Gregorian calendar, following October and preceding December)

fótur_no.etymology: From Old Norse fótr, from Proto-Germanic *fōts, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds.

strax_ao.etymology: Borrowed from Middle Low German, cognate with Swedish strax, Danish straks and dated German stracks.

þvo_so.etymology: From Old Norse þvá, from Proto-Germanic *þwahaną.

sturta_no.etymology: Deverbal from the "pour down" sense of Etymology 1.

From Old Norse tǫnn, from Proto-Germanic *tanþs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dónts.

klæða_so.etymology: From Old Norse klæða, synchronically analyzed as klæði + -a.

seinn_lo.etymology: From Old Norse seinn (whence also Swedish sen), from Proto-Germanic *sainaz, *sainijaz, perhaps related to *sīþuz (“late”), which may imply derivation from some reflex of Proto-Indo-European *seh₁- (“long, lasting”). See also Lithuanian at-sainùs (“careless”).

en: to rest, especially resting or sleeping in a bed
to intend, to plan, to mean to, be going to
to be going to, seem to be going to (indicating a likely course of events)
ætla_so.etymology: Inherited from Old Norse ætla, from Proto-Germanic *ahtilōną (“to strive, think”). Cognate with Swedish ättla, Old Danish ætle.

klára_so.etymology: From klár (“clear, ready”) + -a (verb-forming suffix), literally “to make ready”.

en: room, space (occupied by or intended for a person or thing)
space (the three dimensions in which everything exists and moves)
rúm_no.etymology: From Old Norse rúm, from Proto-Germanic *rūmą, from Proto-Indo-European *rewh₁-.

verð_no.etymology: From Old Norse verðr, from Proto-Germanic *werþaz. Cognate with Old English weorþ (“worth”), English worth.

peningur_no.etymology: From Old Norse peningr, from Proto-Germanic *panningaz. Cognate with English penny.

en: crown, króna, krona, krone, koruna, kroon; any of the so named currencies of Denmark (DKK), Iceland (ISK), Norway (NOK), Sweden (SEK) the Faroe Islands (DKK), the Czech Republic (CZK), Slovakia (SKK) and Estonia (EEK)
crown (part of a tooth above the gum)
króna_no.etymology: Borrowed from Danish krone, ultimately from Latin corōna.

föt_no.etymology: From Old Norse fǫt (“clothes”), the plural of fat (“an article of clothing”), from Proto-Germanic *fatą (“idem”).

skór_no.etymology: From Old Norse skór, from Proto-Germanic *skōhaz, of unclear etymology; possibly a derivation from *skehaną (“to move quickly”), from Proto-Indo-European *skek- (“to move quickly, jump”).

peysa_no.etymology: Likely a clipping of Middle Low German wambeis or Middle Dutch wambeis, for which see Dutch wambuis (“gambeson”) for more.

jakki_no.etymology: From Danish jakke, from Middle Low German and Middle High German jacke, from Middle French jaque.

buxur_no.etymology: Attested since the 16th century. Borrowed from Middle Low German buxe, boxe, from buck (“buck, male goat”) + hose (“trousers”), originally referring to goatskin trousers. Cognate with Danish buks, Swedish byxa, Norwegian bukse, Norwegian Nynorsk bukse, Kashubian bùksë.

kjóll_no.etymology: Borrowed from Danish kjole, contracted from kjortel, cognate to Icelandic kyrtill.

húfa_no.etymology: Inherited from Old Norse húfa. Cognate with Scots how; Old High German hūba,(German Haube); Faroese húgva, Danish and Norwegian Bokmål hue, Norwegian Nynorsk huve and Swedish huva.

en: pouch (pocket in which a marsupial carries its young)
poki_no.etymology: Frin Old Norse poki, from Proto-Germanic *puhô.

stærð_no.etymology: From Old Norse stœrð, from Proto-Germanic *stōriþō, itself a nominal formation from *stōraz (“large”).

gjöf_no.etymology: From Old Norse gjǫf, from Proto-Germanic *gebō.

en: to finance, to bear the cost of

selja_so.etymology: From Old Norse selja (“sell”), from Proto-Germanic *saljaną.

dýr_lo.etymology: From Old Norse dýrr from Proto-Germanic *diurijaz, whence also Old English dīere (English dear), Old High German tiuri. Cognates with Danish dyr, Faroese dýrur, Norwegian Bokmål dyr and Swedish dyr.

stór_lo.etymology: From Old Norse stórr, from Proto-Germanic *stōraz.

lítill_lo.etymology: From Old Norse lítill, from Proto-Germanic *lītilaz. Cognate with Faroese lítil, Danish liden, Norwegian liten, Swedish liten, Elfdalian litn.

nýr_lo.etymology: From Old Norse nýr, from Proto-Germanic *niwjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos (“new”).

gamall_lo.etymology: From Old Norse gamall, from Proto-Germanic *gamalaz.

fallegur_lo.etymology: Attested since the 16th century. Compare Faroese falligur (“beautiful”). Probably derived from the verb falla, as German gefällig.

rauður_lo.etymology: From Old Norse rauðr, from Proto-Germanic *raudaz.

blár_lo.etymology: From Old Norse blár, from Proto-Germanic *blēwaz.

grænn_lo.etymology: From Old Norse grœnn, from Proto-Germanic *grōniz, whence also English green.

gulur_lo.etymology: From Old Norse gulr, from Proto-Germanic *gulaz.

hvítur_lo.etymology: From Old Norse hvítr, from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweytos.

en: under the table (receiving income and not reporting it to the state)
svartur_lo.etymology: From Old Norse svartr, from Proto-Germanic *swartaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swordo- (“dirty, dark, black”).

án_fs.etymology: From Old Norse án, ón, from Proto-Germanic *ēnu.

af_fs.etymology: From Old Norse af, from Proto-Germanic *ab.

hundrað_to.etymology: From Old Norse hundrað, from Proto-Germanic *hundaradą, from *hundą (< Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm) + *radą (“count”).

þúsund_to.etymology: Inherited from Old Norse þúsund, from Proto-Germanic *þūsundī.

eða_st.etymology: From Old Norse eða, from Proto-Germanic *efþau and thus related to Old High German odar, Old English oþþe, Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐌸𐌸𐌰𐌿 (aiþþau).

ávöxtur_no.etymology: From Old Norse ávǫxtr; compare Faroese ávøkstur.

kartafla_no.etymology: Borrowed from Danish kartoffel, from German Kartoffel or Tartuffel, from Italian tartufolo, from tartufo (“truffle”).

banani_no.etymology: Borrowed from Danish banan, from English banana, from a Romance language (either Portuguese banana or Spanish banana), from Wolof banaana.

en: skyr (yogurt-like product made of curdled milk)
skyr_no.etymology:
From Old Norse skyr (“thick curdled milk”, literally “separated”), from skera (“to divide”).
Related to the terms Danish skør (dialect), skørost (dialect), Norwegian Nynorsk skyr (“buttermilk, cultured milk”) or skjør, and Swedish skyr. The Latin term lac concretum (“thick milk”) is found in Tacitus' Germania. Possibly borrowed into English as English scurvy.

sósa_no.etymology: Borrowed from Danish sovs, from French sauce, from Latin salsa, feminine of salsus (“salted”).

salt_no.etymology: From Old Norse salt, from Proto-Germanic *saltą, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂l-, *sḗh₂l, *sáls.

eldhús_no.etymology: From eldur (“fire”) + hús (“house”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk eldhus.

issues: 2 words match; picked so Almennt mál

sjóða_so.etymology: From Old Norse sjóða, from Proto-Germanic *seuþaną.

baka_so.etymology: From Old Norse baka, from Proto-Germanic *bakaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₃g-.

kokkur_no.etymology: Inherited from Old Norse kokkr, from Proto-Germanic *kukkaz.

en: bivalve (mollusc belonging to the taxonomic class Bivalvia, characterized by a shell consisting of two hinged sections)
samloka_no.etymology:
sam- (“co-, syn-”) + loka (“latch, catch, bolt”), apparently referring to the way shellfish "clamp" their shells together.
The "sandwich" sense is due to the resemblance of a sandwich (particularly a submarine sandwich) to various shellfish, especially mussels, with the top and bottom bread slices resembling the shell of a shellfish.

súkkulaði_no.etymology: Borrowed from Danish chokolade, from German Schokolade, from Dutch chocolade, from Spanish chocolate, from Classical Nahuatl chocolātl.

flaska_no.etymology: From Old Norse flaska, from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ. Doublet of fíaskó.

smakka_so.etymology: Borrowed from Middle Low German smaken (“to taste”); see Dutch smaken (“to taste”) for more.

en: satiated, full, having had one’s fill

hollur_lo.etymology: From Old Norse hollr, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz. Cognate with Gothic 𐌷𐌿𐌻𐌸𐍃 (hulþs), Swedish huld.

stofa_no.etymology: From Old Norse stofa, stufa, borrowed from Middle Low German stōve, stūve, Old Saxon *stova, *stuva, from Proto-West Germanic *stubu.

en: bathroom (room with a bathtub and/or shower and usually also a toilet)
toilet (fixture used for urination and defecation)
toilet (room containing one or more toilets but generally no bathtub or shower)
klósett_no.etymology: Borrowed from Danish kloset (“a room for urination and defecation”), from German Klosett, from English closet. Compare English water closet.

íbúð_no.etymology: From í (“in”) + búð (“lived”), literally “that which is lived in”, from the past participle of the verb to reside, to live.

dyr_no.etymology: From Old Norse dyrr, from Proto-Germanic *duriz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwer- (“door, gate”).

en: door (rigid movable pane designed to open and close a doorway)
hurð_no.etymology: From Old Norse hurð, from Proto-Germanic *hurdiz.

gluggi_no.etymology: From Old Norse gluggi. Compare Swedish glugg and Norwegian Bokmål glugge.

en: a key; one of several small, usually square buttons on a typewriter or computer keyboard
lykill_no.etymology: From Old Norse lykill, from Proto-Germanic *lukilaz.

læsa_so.etymology: From Old Norse læsa, from láss (“lock”) (whence Icelandic lás).

lampi_no.etymology: From Old Norse lampi, from Latin lampas, from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás).

skápur_no.etymology: From late Old Norse skáp from Middle Low German schap, from Old Saxon skap, from Proto-West Germanic *skap (“shape”), from Proto-Germanic *skapą.

mynd_no.etymology: Inherited from Old Norse mynd (“shape, form”).

sjónvarp_no.etymology: From sjón (“vision”) + varp (“projection”), modelled after útvarp (“broadcasting, radio”).

en: over there, there (the place being pointed at)
filler word, marking a pause in speech
þarna_ao.etymology: From Old Norse þarna. By surface analysis, þar (“there”, anaphoric adverb) + -na (demonstrative suffix). Compare svo and svona.

hlið_no.etymology: From Old Norse hlið (“side”). Cognate to Old Swedish liþ (“side”).

út_ao.etymology: From Old Norse út, from Proto-Germanic *ūt.

upp_ao.etymology: From Old Norse upp, from Proto-Germanic *upp.

niður_ao.etymology: From Old Norse niðr, from Proto-Germanic *niþer, from Proto-Indo-European *niter. Cognates include Danish and Swedish ned, English nether, Dutch neder, German nieder.

en: to decide, to determine, to resolve
setja_so.etymology: From Old Norse setja, from Proto-Germanic *satjaną.

en: to lay (stones, tiles, a road), to pave
leggja_so.etymology: From Old Norse leggja, from Proto-Germanic *lagjaną.

en: to snatch, to seize, to grab
þrífa_so.etymology: From Old Norse þrífa, from Proto-Germanic *þrībaną. Cognate with English thrive, which came to mean "to take" and thereby "to grow" (reflexive).

laga_so.etymology: Inherited from Old Norse laga (“to prepare, make ready”).

en: to light, start (a fire), turn on (a light); also used of electric appliances and lamps with the preposition á (“on”)

slökkva_so.etymology: From Old Norse sløkkva, from Proto-Germanic *slakwjaną. Probably not related to English slake, which originally meant “to weaken”.

hreinn_lo.etymology: From Old Norse hreinn, from Proto-Germanic *hrainiz.

skyrta_no.etymology: According to Vladimir Orel from *skurti. Cognate to Old Norse skyrta, Middle Low German schorte (“shirt”). From the same source like Albanian shkurt (“short”) and shkurte (“shirt”); which was probably borrowed from a Germanic language, although unlikely.

sokkur_no.etymology: From Old Norse sokkr, from Latin soccus (“slipper”), from Ancient Greek σύκχος (súkkhos, “a kind of shoe”), probably from Phrygian or another language from Asia Minor.

en: a thick winter coat (often with a fur-lined cap); a parka; an anorak
úlpa_no.etymology: From archaic ólpa (“wide coat with cap”), of uncertain origin, though probably from a Proto-Germanic *wulpǭ (“woven garment”), from a Proto-Indo-European *welp- (“to bend, wrap around”), which appears to be a p-extension of *welH- (“to roll”), thus denoting a "rolled-up garment". See also Middle English wlappen (“to wrap”), Sami wuölppo (“woman's garment”), the latter which appears to be borrowed from North Germanic.

trefill_no.etymology: From Old Norse trefill (“tatter, rag”), synchronically analyzable as traf (“fringe, wrapping”) + -ill.

en: glove, mitten (usually knitted or made out of thin material)
vettlingur_no.etymology: From vöttur (“a glove, a mitten”) + -lingur (“diminutive suffix”).

hattur_no.etymology: From Old Norse hǫttr, from Proto-Germanic *hattuz.

en: a dye or paint to colour with
a marker, crayon or colour pencil
litur_no.etymology: From Old Norse litr, from Proto-Germanic *wlitiz, *wlituz (“appearance, look, aspect”), from Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“to see”).

grár_lo.etymology: From Old Norse grár, from Proto-Germanic *grēwaz.

bleikur_lo.etymology: From Old Norse bleikr, from Proto-Germanic *blaikaz. Compare Old English blāc (“pale”). See also bleikja. More at bleak.

taska_no.etymology: From Old Norse taska, from Proto-Germanic *taskǭ.

of_ao.etymology: From Old Norse of-, from Proto-Germanic *uber. The original full form is seen in the prefixed form ofur- (“overly, super, very”). Related to yfir (“above”) and ofan (“from above”).

líta_so.etymology: From Old Norse líta, from Proto-Germanic *wlītaną.

hár_no.etymology: Inherited from Old Norse hár, from Proto-Germanic *hērą.

auga_no.etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ-der.
Proto-Germanic *augô
Proto-Norse *ᚨᚢᚷᚨ (*auga)
Old Norse auga
Icelandic auga
From Old Norse auga, from Proto-Germanic *augô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”). Cognates include Latin oculus, Sanskrit अक्षि (ákṣi), Gothic 𐌰𐌿𐌲𐍉 (augō), Old English ēage, English eye, Scots ee, German Auge, Swedish öga, Danish øje.

en: long (of distance or time or the length of an object)
langur_lo.etymology: From Old Norse langr, from Proto-Germanic *langaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dlongʰos.

stuttur_lo.etymology: From Old Norse stuttr, from Proto-Germanic *stuntaz.

klár_lo.etymology: Borrowed from Middle Low German klar, from Latin clarus (“bright, clear”).

fyndinn_lo.etymology: From finna (“to find; feel”), thus "fount, felt" > "full of sense and wit" > "funny, witty".

stoltur_lo.etymology: Cognates with Danish stolt (“proud”) and Faroese stoltur.

svona_ao.etymology: From Old Norse svána. Composed of svo (“so, thus”) + -na (proximal suffix).

en: bright, shining (describing the sun, moon, day, fire, etc.)
glaður_lo.etymology: From Old Norse glaðr, from Proto-Germanic *gladaz.

hamingjusamur_lo.etymology: From the genitive of Old Norse hamingja (“luck”) + -samur. In Nordic mythology, hamingja was a type of female guardian spirit that accompanied an individual and brought them luck and happiness (the hamingja usually appeared in dreams in the form of an animal) + samur (“same”).

leiður_lo.etymology: From Old Norse leiðr, from Proto-Germanic *laiþaz. Compare German leid, where "einer Sache leid sein" (to be tired of something), still has the same meaning like the Icelandic cognate.

reiður_lo.etymology: From Old Norse reiðr, from older vreiðr, from Proto-Germanic *wraiþaz.

brosa_so.etymology: Inherited from Old Norse brosa (“to smile; a smile”).

hlæja_so.etymology: From Old Norse hlæja, from Proto-Germanic *hlahjaną.

gráta_so.etymology: From Old Norse gráta, from Proto-Germanic *grētaną.

áhyggja_no.etymology: From á (“on”) + hyggja (“(related to) mind”); compare the similar áhugi.

skap_no.etymology: From Old Norse skap, from Proto-Germanic *skapą (“shape, nature, condition”).

snjór_no.etymology: From Old Norse snjór, snjár, snær.

vindur_no.etymology: From Old Norse vindr, from Proto-Germanic *windaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁n̥ts (“blowing”), present participle of *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).

en: the sun (star which illuminates one side of the Earth)
sun (applied to any star or used metaphorically)
sól_no.etymology: From Old Norse sól, from Proto-Germanic *sōl (“sun”).

ský_no.etymology: From Old Norse ský, from Proto-Germanic *skiwją (“cloud, cloud cover”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to cover, conceal”).

jökull_no.etymology: From Old Norse jǫkull, from Proto-Germanic *jekulaz. Diminutive of jaki (“a piece of ice, broken ice”).

en: a waterfall (permanent flow of water over the edge of a cliff)
foss_no.etymology:
Inherited from Old Norse fors.
Cognates: Faroese fossur, Norwegian fors, Danish fors, Swedish fors, English force (in the sense of a waterfall), Middle Low German vorsch and Norn fors.

fjall_no.etymology: From Old Norse fjall, Proto-Germanic *falisaz, from Proto-Indo-European *pels-.

sjór_no.etymology: From Old Norse sær, from Proto-Germanic *saiwiz.

rigna_so.etymology: From Old Norse regna, from Proto-Germanic *regnōną (“to rain”), verbal form of *regną (“rain”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hreǵʰ- (“to flow”).

snjóa_so.etymology: From Old Norse snjóva, from Proto-Germanic *snīwaną.

en: to see, to sense or perceive with one's eyes
to see, to perceive, to spot
sjá_so.etymology: Inherited from Old Norse sjá, séa, from Proto-Germanic *sehwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to see, notice”).

heyra_so.etymology: From Old Norse heyra, from Proto-Germanic *hauzijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱh₂owsyéti.

en: to appear, to bode (a certain way)

mjög_ao.etymology: From Old Norse mjǫk, from Proto-Germanic *mekō, from Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂s; related to mikill (< *mikilaz, derived from a suffixed form of the same Indo-European word).

úti_ao.etymology: From Old Norse úti, from Proto-Germanic *ūtai.

en: located further away from the exit of the house

kannski_ao.etymology: Probably borrowed from Danish kanske (“perhaps”), though related to it regardless. Other cognates include Faroese kanska, Norwegian Nynorsk kanskje, Norwegian Bokmål kanskje, Swedish kanske.

en: an ornamental head on a bridle
the ornamental prow of a ship
höfuð_no.etymology: From Old Norse hǫfuð, from Proto-Germanic *hafudą or *habudą, northern form of *haubudą, from Proto-Indo-European *káput (“head”). More at English head.

en: a person (used only in set phrases)
háls_no.etymology: From Old Norse hals, from Proto-Germanic *halsaz.

eyra_no.etymology: From Old Norse eyra, from the voiced Verner alternant of Proto-Germanic *ausô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ous-.

magi_no.etymology: From Old Norse magi, from Proto-Germanic *magô.

bak_no.etymology: From Old Norse bak, from Proto-Germanic *baką.

en: hand, handwriting (someone's personal style of writing)
hönd_no.etymology: From Old Norse hǫnd, from Proto-Germanic *handuz.

munnur_no.etymology: From Old Norse munnr, from Proto-Germanic *munþaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ment-.

en: to harm, hurt, wound, injure, damage
meiða_so.etymology: From Old Norse meiða, from Proto-Germanic *maidijaną or *maiþijaną.

en: to break (particularly of natural forces relating to the sea) [with preceding accusative ‘person/thing being broken’] (idiomatically translated as “be broken”, “be smashed”, or “break (middle voice)”, with the preceding accusative object as the logical subject)

to cause to break (particularly of natural forces relating to the sea) [with preceding accusative ‘thing doing the breaking’ and following accusative ‘person/thing being broken’] (idiomatically translated as “break” or “smash”, with the preceding accusative object as the logical subject)
brjóta_so.etymology: From Old Norse brjóta, from Proto-Germanic *breutaną.

en: describing a specific feeling; to feel
líða_so.etymology: From Old Norse líða, from Proto-Germanic *līþaną. The senses “suffer, tolerate” may be borrowed from Middle Low German, but derive from the same root in any case.

veikur_lo.etymology: From Old Norse veikr, from Proto-Germanic *waikwaz.

slæmur_lo.etymology: Borrowed from Danish slem, which borrowed it from Middle Low German slim (“bent, crooked”), from Old Saxon *slimb, from Proto-West Germanic *slimb, from Proto-Germanic *slimbaz (“slanted, crooked”). Possibly related to Lithuatian slim̃pti (“to sneak, stroll”).

hraustur_lo.etymology:
From Old Norse hraustr, from Proto-Germanic *hraustaz (“strong, active”).
An older theory by Pokorny derives the Old Norse from Proto-Indo-European *kreu- (“to shake, wave around”), comparing Tocharian A kru (“reed”), Tocharian B kärwats, Lithuanian krutéti (“to move”) (though this is now considered dated).

kvef_no.etymology: From an earlier Proto-Germanic *kwabją, synchronically analyzed as a nominal formation from kvefja (“to suffocate, choke”), see there for more.

en: having a cold, suffering from a cold

hnerra_so.etymology: From the noun hnerri, from Old Norse hnøri, hneri, from the past stem of the verb hnjósa (“to sneeze”) (past hnøri), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hneusaną.

hósta_so.etymology: Inherited from Old Norse hósta, from Proto-Germanic *hwōstōną.

læknir_no.etymology: From Old Norse læknir (“healer”). Equivalent to lækna + -ir.

lyf_no.etymology: From Old Norse lyf, from Proto-Germanic *lubją.

en: to cause to recover (from a disease) [with preceding dative ‘someone’] (idiomatically translated as “recover (from a disease)”, with the dative object as the logical subject)
batna_so.etymology: From Old Norse batna, from Proto-Germanic *batnaną.

vona_so.etymology: From Old Norse vána, from the noun ván (“hope”) (Icelandic von).

reykja_so.etymology: From Old Norse reykja, from Proto-Germanic *raukijaną.

en: to cause to want, to make feel like [with preceding accusative ‘someone’, along with í (+ accusative) ‘something’ or að (+ infinitive) ‘to do something’] (idiomatically translated as “want” or “feel like”, with the preceding accusative object as the logical subject)
to crave, to have a hankering for
langa_so.etymology: From Old Norse langa (“to long for; desire”), from Proto-Germanic *langōną (“to desire; long for”), related to English long, German verlangen. More at long.

áhugamál_no.etymology: Literally, “matter of interest”. From áhugi (“interest”) + mál (“matter”).

skemmta_so.etymology: From either Proto-Germanic *skammatjaną or Proto-Germanic *skammitōną, both from *skammaz (“short, blunt”); the sense development would be "to shorten (the hours)" > "to make time fly (when having fun)" > "to entertain, amuse"". Cognate with Faroese skemta, Norwegian Nynorsk skjemta, Swedish skämta, and Danish skæmte.

frí_no.etymology: From Old Norse frjá, from Proto-Germanic *frijōną, *frijaz, *frijô.

íþrótt_no.etymology: From Old Norse íþrótt, from ið + þróttr (“strength”).

lið_no.etymology: From Old Norse lið, from Proto-Germanic *lidą (“flock, crowd, group”).

spila_so.etymology: Borrowed from Middle Low German spil, from Old Saxon spil, from Proto-West Germanic *spil (“game, dance”).

æfa_so.etymology: Probably ultimately from or related to Proto-Germanic *ōbijaną (“to do, practice”); compare Middle High German uop (“farming, implementation”).

hlaupa_so.etymology: From Old Norse hlaupa, from Proto-Germanic *hlaupaną, from Proto-Indo-European *klewb- (“to spring, stumble”).

synda_so.etymology: From Old Norse sund (“swimming”), from Proto-Germanic *sundą.

en: to bike, cycle (ride a cycle or travel by it)

skíði_no.etymology: From Old Norse skíð, from Proto-Germanic *skīdą.

dansa_so.etymology: From Old Norse dansa, through Old French.

en: to warble, to sing, to chirp
to sound, to ring, to resound
syngja_so.etymology: From Old Norse syngva, syngja, from Proto-Germanic *singwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷʰ-.

leika_so.etymology: From Old Norse leika, from Proto-Germanic *laikaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyg-.

en: game (with some sort of equipment such as playing cards or a board, usually not on a large scale)
play, playing (the act of playing, also music)
spil_no.etymology: Inherited from Old Norse spil (Old West Norse/Old Icelandic), found in Skáld-Helga rímur (15th c.), Borrowed from Middle Low German spil, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *spil (“game”).

skák_no.etymology: From Old Norse skák, from Classical Persian شاه (šāh), from Middle Persian 𐭬𐭫𐭪𐭠 (mlkʾ /⁠šāh⁠/), from Old Persian 𐏋 (XŠ /⁠xšāyaθiya⁠/, “king”).

mála_so.etymology:
From Old Norse mála, from Proto-Germanic *mēlōną, which could be related to *mailą (“spot, blemish, mark”).
Cognate with Finnish maalata, Danish male, German malen (“to paint”) and Swedish måla from Middle Low German mâlen (“to draw, paint”).

bíó_no.etymology: Borrowed from Danish bio, shortened from biograf.

ferðast_so.etymology: From Old Norse ferðask, from Proto-Germanic *fardijōną.

veiða_so.etymology: From Old Norse veiða, from Proto-Germanic *waiþijaną.

en: a job, an occupation, an employment

kennari_no.etymology: From kenna (“to teach”) + -ari (“suffix used to create agent nouns from verbs”).

bók_no.etymology: From Old Norse bók, from Proto-Germanic *bōks.

tölva_no.etymology: A portmanteau word, coined by Sigurður Nordal in 1965 from tala (“number”) + völva (“prophetess”).

orð_no.etymology:
From Old Norse orð, from Proto-Germanic *wurdą, from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰo- (“word”), from Proto-Indo-European *werh₁- (“speak”).
Cognate with Old Frisian word, Old Saxon word, Dutch woord, Old High German wort (German Wort), Swedish ord, Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌳 (waurd), and English word.
The Proto-Indo-European root is also the source of Latin verbum, Lithuanian vardas, and, more distantly, of Ancient Greek εἴρω (eírō, “to say”) and Old Church Slavonic ротити сѧ (rotiti sę, “to swear”) (Russian ротиться (rotitʹsja, “to vow”)).

en: to study something, to learn something
læra_so.etymology: From late Old Norse læra, lǽra, from Old Saxon lērian, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *laizijaną.

lesa_so.etymology: From Old Norse lesa, from Proto-Germanic *lesaną.

skrifa_so.etymology:
From Old Norse skrifa, from Proto-Germanic *skrībaną, a late borrowing from Latin scrībō (“write”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skreybʰ-.
Compare Faroese skriva, Danish skrive, West Frisian skriuwe, Low German schrieven, Dutch schrijven, German schreiben, Swedish skriva.

hlusta_so.etymology: From Old Norse hlusta, equivalent to hlust f (“auditory canal”) + -a (denominal suffix).

en: to do, to perform (e.g. a task)
to win, to triumph in (e.g. a game)
vinna_so.etymology: From Old Norse vinna, from Proto-Germanic *winnaną, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to strive, wish, desire, love”). Related to Faroese vinna, Swedish vinna, Norwegian Bokmål vinne, English win, Dutch winnen, and German gewinnen.

hjálpa_so.etymology: From Old Norse hjalpa, from Proto-Germanic *helpaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelb-, *ḱelp-.

en: to know (by heart), know a skill
kunna_so.etymology: From Old Norse kunna, from Proto-Germanic *kunnaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃-.

en: to cause to differ (by a certain margin) [with dative ‘something’] (idiomatically translated as "differ" with the dative object as the subject)
to cause to make a difference [with um (+ accusative) ‘something’] (idiomatically translated as "make a difference" with the prepositional object as the subject)
muna_so.etymology: From Old Norse muna, from Proto-Germanic *munaną. Cognate with Faroese muna & English mind.

en: to think, to consider, to plan, to decide

erfiður_lo.etymology: From Old Norse erfiðr, synchronically analyzed as an adjectival formation from erfiði (“toil”).

skemmtilegur_lo.etymology: Derived from Old Norse skemtiligr (“amusing, interesting, pleasant”), compare Old Norse óskemtiligr (“dull, uninteresting”), skemtiliga (“amusingly, pleasantly”), skemta (“to amuse, to entertain”), skemtan or skemtun (“entertainment”) and skemtanligr (“amusing, pleasant”). By surface analysis, skemmta + -legur.

en: Icelandic (of or pertaining to Iceland, Icelanders or the Icelandic language)
íslenskur_lo.etymology: From Old Norse íslenzkr, from Ísland.

starf_no.etymology: From Old Norse starf, from starfa (“to work, labour”), from Proto-Germanic *starfą (“labor”), cognate with English starve.

yfirmaður_no.etymology: Inherited from Old Norse yfirmaðr. From yfir (“over”) + maður (“person”).

vakt_no.etymology: From Middle Low German wachte, from Old Saxon wahta, from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō.

en: to turn up, to show up, to come, to appear
mæta_so.etymology: From Old Norse mǿta, from Proto-Germanic *mōtijaną. Compare Norwegian møte, Danish møde, Swedish möta.

opinn_lo.etymology: From Old Norse opinn, from Proto-Germanic *upanaz. Compare Faroese opin, Norwegian open, åpen, Danish åben, Swedish öppen, Dutch open, Low German apen, open, German offen, West Frisian iepen, English open.

en: an order, a row, a sequence
röð_no.etymology: From Old Norse rǫð, from Proto-Germanic *radō.

næstur_lo.etymology: From Old Norse næstr, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwistaz, superlative of *nēhwaz, from Pre-Germanic *h₂nḗḱwos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂neḱ- (“to reach”).

en: a place or position on a list
sæti_no.etymology: From Old Norse sæti, from Proto-Germanic *sētiją. Compare the English seat.

pakki_no.etymology: From Old Norse pakki, possibly borrowed through Middle Low German packe from Old Saxon *pakko, all from Proto-Germanic *pakkô.

sækja_so.etymology: From Old Norse sǿkja, from Proto-Germanic *sōkijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂g- (“to seek out”).

en: to divide, to partition, to cleave
skipta_so.etymology: From Old Norse skipta, from Proto-Germanic *skiftijaną.

greiða_so.etymology: From Old Norse greiða (“to arrange; fit out; comb”), from Proto-Germanic *garaidijaną.

lán_no.etymology: From Old Norse lán, from Proto-Germanic *laihną, from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ-.

en: receipt (written acknowledgement of received goods or money)
transportation ticket; a pass entitling the holder to board a train, a bus, a plane, or other means of transportation.
admission ticket; pass entitling the holder to admission to a show, concert, etc.
miði_no.etymology: From the same root as mið (“middle, mark”); see there for more.

en: to book (include in a written record)
to book (register an order for a hotel room, flight, reserve a table at a restaurant, etc.)

ferð_no.etymology: From Old Norse ferð, from Proto-Germanic *fardiz.

farangur_no.etymology: From fara (“to go”) + -angur, i.e. "the things that one takes with oneself when going somewhere", based on the model of fargagn (“means of transport”).

lest_no.etymology: From Middle Low German last, from Old Saxon *hlast, from Proto-West Germanic *hlasti (“burden, load”).

stöð_no.etymology: From Old Norse stǫð, from standa.

en: a taxi, a taxicab, a cab

gleyma_so.etymology: From Old Norse gleyma (“to be merry; to forget”), from glaumr (whence Icelandic glaumur).

týna_so.etymology: From Old Norse týna, from the root of tjón (“loss, damage”).

en: to give away, to hand over

nú_ao.etymology: From Old Norse nú, from Proto-Germanic *nu (“now”), from Proto-Indo-European *nū (“now”).

þá_ao.etymology: From Old Norse þá (“then”). The conclusive -n has fallen away in the Scandinavian dialects already in the oldest texts.

enn_ao.etymology: From Old Norse enn, from Proto-Germanic *andi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entí.

en: suddenly (happening quickly and with little or no warning)
here (movement), into here, to here, hither
hingað_ao.etymology: From Old Norse hingat, from *hinn veg at.

frétt_no.etymology: From Old Norse frétt, from Proto-Germanic *frihtiz.

saga_no.etymology:
From Old Norse saga, from Proto-Germanic *sagǭ.
Cognate with Old English sagu (English saw); Old Frisian sege; Old High German saga (German Sage); Old Danish saghæ, Old Swedish sagha, Faroese søga, Nynorsk soge, Jutlandic save (“a narrative, a narration, a tale, a report”), Swedish saga. Perhaps related to Lithuanian pasaka.
Compare with segja (“to say, to tell”) and sögn (“a story”).

en: to change, to modify, to alter
breyta_so.etymology:
Inherited from Old Norse breyta, causative of brjóta (“to break”), from Proto-Germanic *breutaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewd-.
Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål brøyte (“to clear snow (off the road)”) and Old English ābrīetan (“to break”).

eyða_so.etymology: From Old Norse eyða, from Proto-Germanic *auþijaną. Related to the adjective auðr (“empty, barren”) ( > Icelandic auður).

en: to visit, to pay a visit
heimsækja_so.etymology: From sækja einhvern heim (“to visit someone”), from Old Norse sœkja heim (“to visit; to attack someone”). Compare Danish hjemsøge.

halda_so.etymology: From Old Norse halda, from Proto-Germanic *haldaną.

en: to get, catch, apprehend (a physical object)
ná_so.etymology: From Old Norse ná, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwāną, related to (or derived from) Proto-Germanic *nēhwaz (“near”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂neḱ- (“to reach”).

deyja_so.etymology: From Old Norse deyja, from Proto-Germanic *dawjaną.

en: to finish, end (bring to an end)
enda_so.etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *h₂ent-
Proto-Indo-European *h₂entíos
Proto-Germanic *andijaz
Old Norse endi
Icelandic endi
Icelandic enda
From endi.

forrit_no.etymology: From for- (“pre-, pro-”) + rit (“writ, writing”). Calque of English program, which is derived from Ancient Greek πρό (pró, “before”) + γράμμα (grámma, “writing”).

tækni_no.etymology:
A neologism derived from tæki (“a tool”) + -ni (nominal suffix). Phono-semantic matching of Danish teknik. Coined by Dr. Björn
Bjarnason from Viðfjörður in 1912.

rafmagn_no.etymology: From raf (“amber”) + magn (“power”), calquing the internationalism electricity, which derives from Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron, “amber”).

þota_no.etymology: A neologism from þotinn, the past participle of the verb þjóta (“rush, dash”).

veira_no.etymology: Said to be coined by Director General of public health Vilmundur Jónsson in 1955 based on feyra (“putridness, mustiness; decay”), with phono-semantic matching of English virus.

hátalari_no.etymology: From hátt (“loud”) + tala (“to talk, to speak”) + -ari (“-er”), a calque of English loudspeaker.

reikistjarna_no.etymology: Coined by Jónas Hallgrímsson, from reika (“to wander”) + stjarna (“star”). Calque of Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer, planet”)

hafa_so.etymology: From Old Norse hafa, from Proto-Germanic *habjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“take, seize”).

en: to cause to occur (a specified weather event) [with það ‘dummy subject’ and accusative ‘weather event’] (usually in the past tense; idiomatic transation depends on the particular weather event)
gera_so.etymology: From Old Norse gera, gøra, gørva, from Proto-Germanic *garwijaną.

en: be going to be, will be
verða_so.etymology: From Old Norse verða, from Proto-Germanic *werþaną.

geta_so.etymology: From Old Norse geta (whence also English get), from Proto-Germanic *getaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“take, seize”). Compare Danish gide, Swedish gitta, English get.

fá_so.etymology: From Old Norse fá, from Proto-Germanic *fanhaną. Doublet of fanga (“to capture, to seize”).

taka_so.etymology: From Old Norse taka, from Proto-Germanic *tēkaną.

vita_so.etymology: From Old Norse vita, from Proto-Germanic *witaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“see”).

gefa_so.etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *gʰebʰ-
Proto-Germanic *gebaną
Old Norse gefa
Icelandic gefa
Inherited from Old Norse gefa, from Proto-Germanic *gebaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰebʰ-.

þurfa_so.etymology: From Old Norse þurfa, from Proto-Germanic *þurbaną.

en: to be allowed, to be permitted, may
to have the strength, to be able
mega_so.etymology: From Old Norse mega, from Proto-Germanic *maganą, from Proto-Indo-European *magʰ-, *megʰ-.

en: to please [with dative ‘experiencer’ and nominative ‘cause’] (idiomatically translated as “like”, with the dative object as the logical subject)
to please [with dative ‘experiencer’ and við (+ accusative) ‘cause’] (idiomatically translated as “like”, with the dative object as the logical subject)
líka_so.etymology: From Old Norse líka, from Proto-Germanic *līkāną.

sitja_so.etymology: From Old Norse sitja, from Proto-Germanic *sitjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“sit”).

standa_so.etymology: From Old Norse standa. from Proto-Germanic *standaną. Cognate with Faroese standa, English stand, Danish stande, Norwegian Nynorsk standa.

liggja_so.etymology: From Old Norse liggja, from Proto-Germanic *ligjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ-.

opna_so.etymology: From Old Norse opna, from Proto-Germanic *upanōną.

en: to stop, to close (a hole, e.g. on a flute) or press down (a string on a violin etc) in order to play a particular note

hringja_so.etymology: From Old Norse hringja, from Proto-Germanic *hringijaną.

en: this, that (referring to both persons and things)
þessi_fn.etymology: From Old Norse [Term?] *þes-, þessi (neuter plural), sjá (nominative), related to and from the same ultimate origin as the irregular inflection of Old Norse sá, a descendant from the likewise irregularly inflected Proto-Germanic *sa. Cognate with Old English þes and Old High German dese.

en: (referring to something or someone which is about to be specified further or has just been mentioned)
sá_fn.etymology: From Old Norse sá, a descendant from Proto-Germanic *sa, from Proto-Indo-European *só. Related to Old Norse sjá.

en: who, which, that (used in the forming of relative clauses)
which (referring to one or several of more than two things or persons)
what, which part (referring to part of a mass or group of things or people considered collectively)
hver_fn.etymology: From Old Norse hverr (from Proto-Germanic *hwarjaz) and *hver (from Proto-Germanic *hwaz), which were conflated in late Old Norse. Most of the inflected forms of *hwaz have since become obsolete, and what remains in form is essentially the descendant of *hwarjaz, but with an extra form for the neuter nominative and accusative singular: hvað from Old Norse hvat.

enginn_fn.etymology: From late Old Norse enginn, from earlier engi, eingi, the ending -inn taken from adjectives. Similarly, the neuter ekkert is from earlier ekki (“nothing”) by analogy with hvert (“each”, neuter) E(i)ngi is a fusion of einn (“one”) + -gi (“not”).

annar_fn.etymology: From Old Norse annarr, from the Proto-Germanic *anþeraz; whence also English other.

líka_ao.etymology: Inherited from Old Norse líka. See líkur.

vel_ao.etymology: From Old Norse vel, from Proto-Germanic *wela.

bara_ao.etymology: Borrowed from Danish bare (“barely, only”). First attested in the 18th c.. Compare Swedish bara.

aftur_ao.etymology: From Old Norse aptr, from Proto-Germanic *aftrą.

heima_ao.etymology: From Old Norse heima. Cognate with Swedish hemma (“at home”).

heim_ao.etymology: From Old Norse heim (“home, homewards”), the accusative form of heimr (“abode, world, land”), from Proto-Germanic *haimaz.

að_st.etymology: From Old Norse at (“that”). From Proto-Germanic *þat (“that”). Cognate with Old English þæt, Gothic 𐌸𐌰𐍄𐌰 (þata).

sem_st.etymology: From Old Norse sem (“as, like”), possibly from Proto-Germanic *samaz (“same, alike”).

ef_st.etymology: From Old Norse ef, from Proto-Germanic *jabai.
